headline: AI commentator GOLAZO screams about your sourdough like it's the World Cup final
summary: GOLAZO uses Google Gemini and ElevenLabs to generate and vocalize over-the-top sports commentary for any moment you describe, from chess victories to rising sourdough.
details: GOLAZO is an AI hype commentator designed to narrate any moment of your life as if it were a World Cup final. It takes a user's description of an event and generates an enthusiastic, over-the-top commentary.

The system leverages Google AI's Gemini 2.0 Flash for generating the commentary text, which streams word-by-word onto the screen. ElevenLabs' eleven_multilingual_v2 provides the voice, tuned for excited delivery.
An example commentary describes a grandpa's chess victory: "Grandpa — seventy-eight years young, cardigan flapping like a cape — slides the rook home! He's done it again! CHECKMAAAAAAATE!"

The project aims to bring the passion of sports commentary to everyday, untelevised moments, including kids' leagues, grassroots matches, or for visually impaired fans. It emphasizes that every moment, especially the small ones, deserves a voice.
Technically, GOLAZO is a single index.html file with no frameworks, build steps, or backend. It calls the Gemini generateContent REST API directly from the browser using the user's own free key.
The design mimics a broadcast, featuring chalk white, pitch green, and ticker yellow, with a scrolling ticker and a blinking REC dot. Commentary types out at broadcast pace to enhance the event feel.
A crucial prompt engineering rule for Gemini is "Never mock the smallness of the moment," ensuring sincere and believing commentary rather than ironic. This sincerity is central to the product.

ElevenLabs' voice settings were specifically tuned (stability 0.35, style 0.7) to achieve a loose, fast, and excited delivery, moving away from a standard newsreader tone. The multilingual model supports authentic-sounding commentary in different languages.
The last eight commentaries are saved locally as "Match Highlights," allowing users to replay their celebrated moments. The developer noted that the hardest bug encountered was CSS, not the AI.
caption:

headline: Learn Embeddings by Building a Resume-to-Project Matcher
summary: This tutorial makes the often-abstract steps of embedding-based retrieval visible by guiding you through building a simple resume-to-project matcher. It covers vector normalization, similarity scoring, and analyzing results without needing an API key.
details: Embedding demos often abstract key steps. This tutorial makes the process visible by building a small matcher, demonstrating how to normalize vectors, compute scores, rank candidates, and inspect failure cases. It uses fixed vectors, so no API key is required.

Cosine similarity measures direction, not absolute truth or skill. The example uses four coordinates for reproducible math, emphasizing that real systems require a single embedding model with recorded name and version.

The guide instructs users to create 20 project descriptions and five synthetic resumes. Before retrieval, label relevant projects to calculate recall at 3, which measures how many labeled relevant projects appear in the top three results.

Inspect misses for issues like vocabulary, language, seniority, negation, or overemphasis on prestigious terms. Emphasize not using demographic attributes and that embeddings should support discovery, not make employment decisions, ensuring review paths for candidates.

Experiment with removing normalization to observe changes in ranking due to vector magnitude. Add a zero vector to verify explicit failure cases and compare different model versions using the same labeled set.

The public MonkeyCode repository describes project requirements and AI tasks, suggesting embedding-based discovery could be relevant for repositories or tasks. This example is purely for teaching and not a MonkeyCode feature claim.
